q: Make the case for Robertson to a buyer who dismisses it as bulk country.
accept: lime rich alkaline soils chardonnay and cap classique de wetshof graham beck
limestone on the breede river gives chardonnay acidity
de wetshof pioneered chardonnay graham beck built sparkling here
alkaline lime soils and diurnal swing despite the heat
ans: Robertson is the Cape's limestone district: lime-rich, alkaline soils along the Breede River, genuinely unusual in a country of granite, shale and sandstone, and the reason Chardonnay and Cap Classique settled here rather than staying in the co-operative trade. Danie de Wet's De Wetshof led the Cape's serious Chardonnay from the late 1970s and early 1980s — a period when much of what had been planted in South Africa under the name Chardonnay turned out to be Auxerrois, a scandal that set the variety back years. Graham Beck built its sparkling house here; Springfield's wild-fermented, unfiltered Méthode Ancienne makes the terroir argument in the glass. It is hot and dry and irrigation from the Breede is not optional, but the lime and the strong diurnal swing off the mountains deliver the acidity, and the district is also the Cape's muscadel heartland.
exp: The persuasive move is geological: name the lime, then name the three producers who monetised it. Robertson also lets you tell the Auxerrois story, which is a favourite oral aside and shows you know how young the Cape's clean plant material really is.

q: Trace how Mendoza is watered, from the Andes to the vine row, and name the risk that now dominates the region's planning.
accept: andean snowmelt through rivers and acequias flood irrigation then drip with snowpack decline the risk
snowmelt fed canals flood irrigation now drip and a shrinking snowpack
a desert irrigated from andean snowmelt facing declining snowpack and water rights limits
ans: Mendoza is desert — 200 to 250 mm of rain — so essentially every vine is irrigated, and the water is Andean snowmelt carried by the Mendoza, Tunuyán, Diamante and Atuel rivers. Pre-Hispanic Huarpe canals were extended into the colonial and nineteenth-century acequia network, and rights are administered by the Departamento General de Irrigación, which allocates by property rather than by need. Traditional flood irrigation — surco and manto — still runs the older low-lying vineyards of Maipú and eastern Mendoza; it is cheap, leaches accumulated salts, and suits the wide-spaced parral. Newer high-altitude Uco plantings use drip fed by reservoirs and boreholes, which permits deficit irrigation timed to véraison, much closer spacing, and precise control of vigour. The dominant risk is a declining Andean snowpack over recent decades, compounded by falling water tables where boreholes have proliferated, so a parcel's water right — not its soil — increasingly decides whether it can be planted at all.
exp: No part of Mendoza can ripen a crop on rainfall; the whole industry is a hydraulic project, and that is the single fact that organises its geography. The flood-versus-drip distinction also explains style: flood-irrigated old parral gives volume and dilution, drip-fed Uco slopes give concentration.

q: Carmenère is easy to name and hard to grow. Explain its viticultural demands, how Chilean growers manage them, and the sites you would cite.
accept: very late ripening with pyrazines needs warm sites like peumo in cachapoal
ripens weeks after merlot managed by water stress and warm clay sites peumo apalta
late ripening green pepper risk devigorate and plant warm sites
ans: It ripens very late — two to three weeks after Merlot, often into late April or May — so it needs a warm site that also warms early, with a long dry autumn. Picked short it shows aggressive methoxypyrazine, green pepper and hard herbaceous tannin; picked too late it goes jammy and loses acidity, so the harvest window is narrow. It is vigorous and must be devigorated: low-fertility ground, clay that meters water, controlled water stress after véraison, restrained nitrogen, and leaf removal in the fruit zone for light rather than heat. Chile's advantage is that most vines are own-rooted, so rootstock cannot be used to solve vigour and site selection does the work. Cite Peumo in Cachapoal as the benchmark, then Apalta, warm inland Colchagua and the warmer sectors of Maipo. In the glass: red fruit with soy, tomato leaf and sweet spice over a firm, faintly herbal finish. Most producers now blend it into Cabernet rather than bottle it varietally, which is the honest verdict — Carmenère is a warm-site specialist, not a national grape.
exp: The 1994 identification solved a naming problem and created a farming problem: blocks planted as Merlot had been picked on Merlot's date for decades. Almost everything green in 1990s Chilean 'Merlot' was a harvest-date error, not a fault of the grape.

q: Explain Torrontés: how many varieties bear the name, their parentage, where each matters, and the winemaking pitfall.
accept: three varieties riojano sanjuanino and mendocino from criolla chica crossed with muscat of alexandria
riojano is the best from cafayate muscat parentage avoid skin contact
three torrontes with muscat of alexandria parentage riojano is the quality one
ans: Three distinct varieties share the name. Torrontés Riojano is the quality one — La Rioja province and, above all, Salta's Cafayate — and DNA has shown it to be a natural cross of Criolla Chica, which is País and Mission, with Muscat of Alexandria. Torrontés Sanjuanino shares that parentage, is coarser and more neutral, and is grown in San Juan. Torrontés Mendocino is a separate cross also involving Muscat of Alexandria, the least aromatic of the three, found in Mendoza and Río Negro. None is related to Galicia's Torrontés. The pitfall follows from the parentage: Muscat supplies an intense floral, citrus-peel perfume that the palate reads as sweetness, while Criolla supplies low acidity and phenolic bitterness — so over-ripening, extended skin contact or warm fermentation produces a soapy, bitter, flabby wine that smells sweet and finishes hard. The modern answer is high-altitude fruit for natural acidity, early picking, cool whole-cluster pressing, minimal or no maceration, cool fermentation, no oak, and bottling dry and young. Colomé, El Esteco, Susana Balbo and Piattelli are the references.
exp: The parentage explains the whole grape: Muscat gives the nose, Criolla gives the phenolics and the low acid. Altitude and restraint in the cellar are the only two levers that keep the wine tasting dry.

q: Present Uruguay as a wine country: its regulatory categories, where the vineyards actually are, and what its producers are doing with Tannat now.
accept: inavi regulates with vcp and vc categories canelones is the heartland and tannat is softened by micro-oxygenation
vcp quality tier two thirds in canelones with maldonado and rivera growing tannat handled gently
inavi vcp category canelones maldonado garzon tannat plus albarino
ans: INAVI regulates the industry, and the label distinction that matters is VCP — Vino de Calidad Preferente, the quality tier, made from approved vinifera varieties and bottled in small format — against VC, Vino Común, the everyday bulk category still sold in demijohns and cartons domestically. Geographically, roughly two-thirds of the vineyard sits in Canelones just north of Montevideo, with Montevideo, San José and Colonia adjoining; the growth stories are Maldonado on the Atlantic, where Bodega Garzón and Alto de la Ballena work granitic ballast soils in a genuinely maritime climate, and Rivera on the Brazilian border, where sandstone and a drier continental climate give riper, softer fruit. Total plantings are small — around 6,000 hectares — so Uruguay competes on identity, not volume. Tannat arrived with Basque immigrants in the 1870s through Pascual Harriague, and the old massal 'Harriague' material now sits beside French INRA clonal selections that are finer-boned. Modern handling is about tannin management rather than extraction: shorter macerations, micro-oxygenation, concrete and larger or older oak, and blending in Merlot, Cabernet Franc or Pinot Noir. Albariño is the credible white and Maldonado is proving it.
exp: Humidity is the real constraint: Atlantic rain at harvest drives lyre and open canopy training, aggressive leaf work and rigorous sorting. That, far more than oak or clone, is why Uruguayan Tannat tastes gentler than Madiran's.
